newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Crude Outlook - only modest price retreat seen.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Crude Outlook - only modest price retreat seen.

text.p: Supply concerns are seen as a key factor in maintaining U.S. benchmark crude prices above $19.00 a barrel this week, despite pressure from a softening unleaded gasoline sector, analysts said Monday.
September light crude futures were down around 20 cents from Friday at $19.80-90 a barrel at midday Monday, with a weaker gasoline sector leading energy futures lower.
Crude prices, however, were not expected to fall drastically, mainly due to supply concerns and the fact gasoline has risen much more sharply than crude in the recent market rally.
"There's a lot of room for the crude in the crack spreads. September cracks could come down $2.00 a barrel and be fairly valued," said William Brown, president of W.H. Brown & Co in New York.

On the supply front, cash prices were undperinned by last week's news that Canada's Interprovincial Pipeline (IPL) would be slicing September crude throughput to the U.S. Midwest by some 141,000 barrels per day, or nearly 10 percent of its usual rate.
Sour cash barrels in the U.S. Gulf gained the most from the disruption, with the discount narrowing by some 15 cents to a $1.10 discount against the September benchmark on Monday.

Sweet barrels continued to hold a 20 cents-plus premium for Light Louisiana Sweet/St. James, and was seen remaining around that area due to tight Brent-WTI arb and lack of other light foreign crude in the Gulf.
In foreign cash crude trade, buyers and sellers were expected to begin winding down their September activity this week and start looking toward October.
Robust downstream margins have encouraged refiners to snap up September barrels without delay.
"I think people are feeling smug about these margins. They have things pretty much wrapped up," a trader for a Gulf Coast refiner said.
North Sea Brent crude was expected to remain elusive in the Gulf, at least for now, reflecting the narrow trans-Atlantic arbitrage, traders said.
Brent was pegged at a notional level of around parity to October WTI, considered pricey compared to domestic and regional alternatives, traders said.
Colombian Cusiana, for example, traded actively last week at $1.05 to $1.10 under October WTI for September loading.

Concerns over possible delays in September liftings of Cusiana as a result of apparent operational hiccups were still being played out Monday morning. Details remained sketchy, but buyers were expecting modest delays and a possible reduction in the number of cargoes still available for September.
October foreign activity kicked off late last week with the sale of Ecuadoran Oriente crude to an East Coast refiner for October 5-10 delivery.
The cargo was sold at an equivalent to around November WTI minus $3.05 a barrel, traders said.
